compression.title: HathiTrust Digital Library
compression.lede: is a digital library administered by the University of Michigan: research-library volumes digitized through Google Books, the Internet Archive and member libraries, more than 18 million in 2024, searchable in full text and shown by copyright status; Authors Guild v. HathiTrust held the search fair use, and the census of the training layer ties none of its volumes to training.

sentences.text: The HathiTrust Digital Library, or HathiTrust, is a digital library: a large-scale collaborative repository of digital content from research libraries, administered by the University of Michigan, and catalogued among American digital libraries, full-text scholarly online databases and mass digitization.

Its collection is of books, journals and government documents digitized from libraries around the world and dated from 1500 to the present: content digitized through Google Books and the Internet Archive, beside collections that member libraries digitized themselves, aggregated in one shared repository; the census keeps it apart from Google Books on that ground and records the Internet Archive as a source it uses.

In September 2024 it comprised more than 18 million volumes, 6.7 million of them in the public domain in the United States; the University of Michigan Library gives the public domain as more than a third of the collection and the items preserved as more than 17 million, and the library's research guide quotes HathiTrust's own figure of 18+ million digitized items.
Its name is the Hindi word for elephant, from the Sanskrit hastin, an animal famed for its long-term memory, and it is a distinct entity from HATII.

HathiTrust was founded in October 2008 by the twelve universities of the Committee on Institutional Cooperation and the eleven libraries of the University of California, its infrastructure put in place at the University of Michigan, which has scanned and deposited more than 4.8 million items.

It is a nonprofit collaborative of academic and research libraries, owned as a university consortium with the University of Michigan as its parent: as of 2024 more than 219 research libraries across the United States, Canada and Europe, under a shared governance structure, with costs shared by the participating libraries and library consortia.
Its executive director is Mike Furlough, who succeeded the founding director John Wilkin after Wilkin stepped down in 2013.

Its Shared Print Program is a distributed collective collection whose participating libraries have committed to retaining almost 18 million monograph volumes for 25 years, three-quarters of its digital book holdings.

What a reader may see follows copyright: items in the public domain, more than a third of the collection, are fully available for everyone, while many items are protected by copyright and cannot be viewed in full without the express permission of the copyright holder.

Its copyright policy, as Wikipedia quotes it for 2021, says that protected works cannot ordinarily be displayed in large portions without permission and that access to a work is restricted until its copyright or permission status can be established; the census knows the policy only through that quotation and, on that restriction, counts the library outside the open full-text libraries for works in copyright.

Access also turns on where the reader is, and the sources date the line differently: Wikipedia quotes the policy as restricting users outside the United States from works published outside the United States after and including 1896, and the University of Michigan's guide quotes HathiTrust's web site as estimating 1898 the earliest date at which foreign works may still be in copyright, so that works published abroad from 1898 through 1928 are open to United States IP addresses and closed to others.

Access turns as well on affiliation: a member's community gains additional access by logging in, and at the University of Michigan logged-in users can download complete public-domain books, where guests download one page at a time.

A volume, a digitized book or other publication, is viewed in PageTurner, the site's web application, in which a reader can navigate a publication, download a PDF of it and view its pages one at a time, scrolling, flipping or as thumbnails.

Through the Emergency Temporary Access Service, users of member libraries can in special situations, such as a library's closure for a public health emergency, obtain lawful access to copyright digital materials in place of the physical books their library holds.
Patrons with print disabilities can obtain downloaded copies of anything in the collection through its Accessible Text Request Service.

Its discovery services include full-text search across the entire repository: researchers search the catalogue's descriptive data, the contents of digitized items, or both, and works still under copyright carry a "Limited (search-only)" status within which a reader can still search for key terms.

The census reads the record as answering whether a volume is held, by full-text search, whether its pages may be shown or only searched, and the scale of the holdings, and it ran no search of its own.

In September 2011 the Authors Guild sued HathiTrust, alleging massive copyright violation, and in October 2012 a federal court found HathiTrust's use of books scanned by Google to be fair use under US law, its opinion resting on the transformativeness doctrine.

The Second Circuit largely affirmed the decision on 10 June 2014, finding that providing search and accessibility for the visually impaired were grounds to consider the service transformative and fair use, and remanded to the lower court whether the plaintiffs had standing over HathiTrust's library preservation copies.

The census reads Authors Guild v. HathiTrust, as Wikipedia reports it, as the record's precedent for a machine reading of whole books whose product is a finding, search, while the pages stay closed; in its record, what an apparatus makes from a work there is a full-text search index the courts held transformative and fair use.

Computational analysis of the volumes was the separate service of the HathiTrust Research Center, established in 2011 as a partnership of Indiana University, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and HathiTrust to enable computational analysis of the library, which supported scholars using text and data mining methods in educational and non-profit research; the census holds the Center as a part of the library and as a distinct entity.

In October 2024 HathiTrust's executive director announced that funding for the Center would cease at the end of 2026, when it will be formally closed; its services were discontinued on 30 September 2026, its accounts, algorithms and data capsules with them, some of its resources remain usable without an account, and access to the Digital Library remains open.

The census of the training layer asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it, and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception; it admits a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds, and its anchors are #186 and #1543.
It enters HathiTrust in its corpora area, the collections, crawls and datasets whose texts enter machine training, as infrastructure and as a record of type library, its question holding and access.

Its saved sources say nothing of training use and tie none of the library's volumes to model training, whether a work keeps its author's name there is not recorded, and the census does not record the library as a training corpus.
The census reads HathiTrust in three layers kept apart: holdings, access restricted where copyright status cannot be established, and computational availability, the Research Center's, now ended.

The archive's Originals Library has met HathiTrust as a holder of open witnesses its sessions could not reach: on 15 October 2026 a seating found HathiTrust not reachable from its workspace for Pound's public-domain first printings of the Cantos, a seating of 27 October 2026 queued Langston Hughes's Fine Clothes to the Jew (1927), whose one open scan is at HathiTrust, as unreachable, and on 30 October 2026 HathiTrust, holding Cornell's volumes 36–37 of the Monatshefte in full view, refused the seating's requests with a Cloudflare challenge and a block page.

Other witnesses the archive seated came by way of HathiTrust: its first edition of The Souls of Black Folk is the Northwestern University copy (HathiTrust ien.35556032538837) uploaded to the Internet Archive, and its Tribüne volume is the University of Michigan copy digitized by Google, held by reference via HathiTrust and the Internet Archive, which HathiTrust records as pdus, public domain in the United States, full view.
The archive's bibliography places its author's doctoral dissertation, Strange New Canons (University of Michigan, 2013), at a HathiTrust catalogue record.

An earlier archive paper classes large text archives such as HathiTrust as having scale and no internal architecture, "collections, not systems", which a summarizer describes by what is in them without traversing how they work; the archive gives the native frame of digital libraries as collections, discovery, preservation and services evaluated as connected functions.

HathiTrust's own about page at hathitrust.org refused the census's fetch with HTTP 403 and a challenge page, so the census quotes nothing in the resource's own words and cites Wikipedia, whose article was last edited on 19 October 2026, and the Research Center's page for its fields; the University of Michigan's guide, last updated on 24 August 2026, quotes HathiTrust's site.

Wikipedia's infobox gives the library as launched in October 2008 and active, partially commercial, written in Perl and Java, with revenue projected at US$3,777,445 for 2019 and a content licence of "Public domain (with restrictions on Google scans), various".

Asked for "HathiTrust Digital Library" in Google AI Mode on 1 November 2026, at a new address, the composer said what the library is, who founded and runs it, how large it is, where its scans come from and what each kind of user may do with them, through seven inline source chips and no cards; the Capture Registry found the repository composed at its grain, with its access tiers, its founding and administration in agreement with Wikipedia.

The registry also found that the composition made the public domain fully available to anyone worldwide, dropping the United States condition; added Microsoft to the sources of the scans, on no saved HathiTrust source; offered the Research Center as a working service a month after its services ended; gave search and the accessibility service as features without the ruling that holds them; and named the University of Michigan and partner libraries, no person and no founders.

CAP-1-07.quote: The innocent reading first. Asked for the library by name in AI Mode, the composer says what it is, who founded and runs it, how large it is, where its scans come from and what each kind of user may do with them, and offers instructions for search or text mining.

CAP-1-12.quote: No source cards: seven inline chips (HathiTrust, Wikipedia, University of Michigan Library, YouTube).

CAP-1-13.quote: The operator's note in the paste ('no popup. ai mode:'): no Overview popup, the run in AI Mode.

CAP-1-08.quote: The repository composed at its grain, with its access tiers, from its own site and the Michigan library guide.

CAP-1-01.quote: 'Founded in 2008 and administered by the University of Michigan' agrees with Wikipedia ('administered by the University of Michigan', 'founded in October 2008').

CAP-1-09.quote: 'HATHITRUST DIGITAL LIBRARY' IN AI MODE — THE REPOSITORY AND ITS ACCESS TIERS AT THEIR GRAIN; ITS RESEARCH CENTER OFFERED IN THE PRESENT TENSE A MONTH AFTER ITS SERVICES ENDED; THE FAIR-USE RULING NOT CARRIED

CAP-1-02.quote: 'Over a third of the collection (roughly 7 million volumes) is in the public domain' rounds Wikipedia's 'more than 18 million volumes, including 6.7 million in the public domain in the United States', and drops 'in the United States', the condition on which the census row's international restriction rests ('access is also restricted for users outside the United States to works published outside the United States after and including 1896'); the composition's public domain is 'fully available for anyone worldwide'.

CAP-1-03.quote: THE SOURCES OF THE SCANS. 'the Google Books Project, the Internet Archive, Microsoft, and member institutions' local scanning projects.' Wikipedia: 'content digitized via Google Books and the Internet Archive digitization initiatives, as well as content digitized locally by libraries.' Microsoft is on no saved HathiTrust source; the census row's Internet Archive evidence records Microsoft's Live Search Books as a contributor to the Internet Archive.

CAP-1-04.quote: THE RESEARCH CENTER IN THE PRESENT TENSE. 'HathiTrust Research Center (HTRC): Offers text-mining and computational analysis tools for researchers to perform advanced data analysis across the entire digital corpus.' The HTRC home page, saved the same day: 'HTRC has discontinued its services as of September 30, 2026. HTRC accounts are no longer available.' and 'HTRC Algorithms and Data Capsule services have also been discontinued.' The follow-up offers 'precise instructions on how to use their Advanced Search or text-mining tools'. The census row gives the Research Center's computational analysis as 'ended 30 September 2026'.

CAP-1-05.quote: The composition gives the search and the Accessible Text Request Service ('Patrons with certified print disabilities') as features, and Authors Guild v. HathiTrust, the ruling that holds them, is absent.

CAP-1-06.quote: NO PERSON AND NO FOUNDERS. The census row names the executive director, 'The executive director of HathiTrust is Mike Furlough,', the 219 member libraries and the founders, 'the twelve universities of the Committee on Institutional Cooperation and the eleven libraries of the University of California'. The composition names partner universities only as places to log in ('University of Michigan, University of Wisconsin, University of Calgary, or even NYPL cardholders') and no person.

CAP-1-10.quote: The University of Michigan and partner libraries named, no person; sources chipped inline, no cards.
